query: Which material can be used for lightweight and superior comprehensive performance, and why?

generation.hypothesis: An Al-rich CoCrFeNi high-entropy alloy (e.g., with a high aluminum content such as Al1.5CoCrFeNi) will yield a lightweight material with superior overall performance because the increased aluminum reduces the density while inducing a beneficial dual-phase microstructure that enhances strength, ductility, and corrosion resistance.
generation.material_initial_state: As-cast CoCrFeNi high-entropy alloy with low aluminum content (e.g., Al0.1CoCrFeNi) exhibiting a single-phase FCC structure and higher density.
generation.intervention: Increase the aluminum content during alloy synthesis (targeting compositions around Al1.5CoCrFeNi) to promote phase evolution and density reduction.
generation.conditions: Processing under standard casting and homogenization conditions at ambient to moderately elevated temperatures, with subsequent conventional mechanical testing (tensile, hardness, corrosion tests).
generation.structural_mediator: The emergence of a dual-phase microstructure consisting of an FCC matrix and ordered BCC (or B2) precipitates induced by high mixing entropy and lattice distortion.
generation.mechanism: Aluminum, being lighter than the other metallic elements, decreases overall density while its higher content promotes transformations that result in a finer microstructural dispersion (through precipitate or ordering effects) that enhances mechanical strength and ductility, as well as corrosion resistance.
generation.predicted_outcome: Compared to a low-Al counterpart (e.g., Al0.1CoCrFeNi), the Al-rich alloy is predicted to exhibit a lower density (approaching ~6.9 g/cm³ instead of ~8.1 g/cm³) along with improved strength, ductility, and corrosion resistance, making it more suitable for lightweight, high-performance structural applications.
generation.baseline: A conventional CoCrFeNi HEA with low aluminum content, which has a higher density and potentially inferior mechanical properties due to its single-phase structure.
generation.boundary: The beneficial effects are expected within a range of aluminum additions that do not trigger excessive phase segregation or embrittlement; performance might vary under extreme thermal cycling or in highly corrosive environments.
generation.uncertainty: The optimal aluminum content for balancing weight reduction and mechanical performance is not precisely determined, and long-term stability under service conditions requires further evaluation.

falsification_experiment.design: Synthesize a series of AlxCoCrFeNi alloys with varying aluminum content (e.g., x = 0.1, 0.75, and 1.5) under identical processing conditions. Characterize the microstructure and measure density, tensile properties, ductility, and corrosion resistance.
measurements: Corrosion testing under simulated service environments
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the Al-rich alloy (e.g., with x = 1.5) does not demonstrate a statistically significant reduction in density combined with equal or superior mechanical and corrosion performance compared to the low-Al version, then the hypothesis that increased aluminum produces a lightweight, high-performance alloy is falsified.

cited_evidence.text: In this paper, the impact of mechanical alloying (MA) and spark plasma sintering (SPS) on the phase evolution and mechanical properties development of CoCrFeNiTi high–entropy alloys (HEAs) was investigated. The microstructure and properties of the material were examined, using X-ray diffraction (XRD) for phase identification, scanning electron microscopy (SEM) for surface morphology observation, transmission electron microscopy (TEM) for microstructural analysis, and hardness testing to evaluate mechanical performance. The milled powder exhibited nanocrystalline solid solution microstructure with grain sizes below 48 nm, composed of 83% face–centered cubic (FCC) and 17% body–centered cubic (BCC) phases. Mechanically, the bulk CoCrFeNiTi alloy exhibited exceptional strength attributes, as evidenced by a Vickers hardness value reaching 675 Hv, along with a compressive strength of 1894 MPa and a yield stress of 1238 MPa. High–entropy alloys (HEAs) have had remarkable progress and advancement since their development by Professor Yeh in 2004. The term “high–entropy alloy” generally refers to a single–phase solid solution alloy with a simple crystal structure composed of five or more elements, with an atomic percentage ranging from 5% to 35% [ [1] , [2] , [3] ]. Given their superior hardness, exceptional strength, resistance to corrosion, and a multitude of additional benefits, HEAs have became a new type of alloy material that has received a great deal of attention in the research field during recent years and the hot point of many researches [ [4] , [5] , [6] , [7] ]. The high–entropy alloy composed of five elements–Cobalt (Co), Chromium (Cr), Iron (Fe), Nickel (Ni), and Titanium (Ti)–in equimolar or nearly equimolar proportions exhibited a simple solid solution structure and favorable plasticity and machinability. However, it suffered from a relatively low hardness and strength [ [8] , [9] , [10] ]. The existing research lacked a comprehensive and thorough understanding of the microstructure and deformation dynamics of the CoCrFeNiTi high–entropy alloy.

The fields of aerospace and fossil energy have benefited from decades of the development of Ni-base superalloys. However, to obtain further efficiency gains and environmental friendliness, developing new materials with inexpensive, light, and strong characteristics is required. Numerous efforts can be found in the development of novel ferritic superalloys containing a disordered body-centered-cubic (BCC) matrix with ordered B2 and/or L2 1 precipitates due to their good creep resistance at elevated temperatures and relatively lower densities [1] , [2] . However, these emerging precipitation-strengthened ferritic alloys still face some drawbacks, such as the low high-temperature strength and not lightweight, which limit their applications. To overcome these issues, new alloy-design strategies are required. Recently, the concept of high-entropy alloys (HEAs) or multi-principal-element alloys (MPEAs) has revolutionized the traditional alloy-design strategy, using multi-principal components (≥5) instead of one or two key components [3] – [10] .
